chapters.label: HOW WE KNOW IT IS SAFE
WHEN IT FAILS, WHAT PASS MEANS

lines.caption: Eight a.m. A message from the research team. Was last night's run really offline? And can we trust the result?
By the end of this film, you can answer that in one breath. Here is the whole picture.
Three islands. On the left, the connected mainland: the internet, and GitLab, the official home of our pipelines.
In the middle, the vault: private AWS storage.
On the right, the sealed island, where the science runs. There is no bridge to the mainland. Only one private pipe, from the vault.
Everything starts on the mainland. A GitLab Runner takes a pinned nf-core workflow, for example Sarek, for germline variant calling.
It discovers every container image the workflow needs, and collects the plugins, reference files and test data.
Security scans check the code and the images. They report every finding to the team, without blocking the release on their own.
Then the crate is packed: one bundle, with a SHA-256 fingerprint for every file.
The crate crosses to the vault. The bundle lands in Amazon S3.
Each container image is copied into private Amazon ECR by its digest: its exact identity, not a tag that can move.
Then a readback checks everything again, from AWS itself, and only then is the release registered. Only a registered release can run.
A reviewed request starts AWS CodePipeline. Ten checks, in order, every time.
Source and intake first. Then the bundle, the data and the images, each matched to its fingerprint. Then a preflight on the host, the offline run, the results, and the report.
Each check runs in AWS CodeBuild, and reaches the host only through Systems Manager.
The host lives in a private subnet with no route to the internet. No NAT, no internet gateway, no public IP.
We tested it. The internet timed out. S3 and ECR answered, through private endpoints only.
Inside, Nextflow runs offline, and every task runs in Podman, with the network off and image pulls disabled.
So what if a task tries to reach out? There is nowhere to go. The run stops at stage eight, and says FAIL. Loudly. Never silently.
Your move is simple. Open the report, see which stage failed, and share it. Nothing ever runs half connected.
And when you see PASS, all ten checks passed, offline, with evidence you can show.
Five pipeline lanes have passed this way, including three Sarek workflows.
Next, the same release travels further. Promotion copies it, by digest, to other AWS accounts. It has passed five times in development.
The goal: researchers on Lifebit CloudOS, in subnets with no internet, reading only from these private stores, with CodeCommit for the pipeline code.
So when the research team asks, you can tell them: yes, it was offline. Here is the proof.
Prepare once. Run sealed. Prove it.
